sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** The OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) Model is a seven-layer conceptual framework that describes how data moves from a physical wire on one computer to an application on another, with each layer handling a distinct concern: addressing, reliability, formatting, or application semantics.
The OSI Model was published by the ISO in 1984 as a reference architecture for building interoperable networks. While the actual internet runs on the leaner TCP/IP model (Topic 2), OSI remains the universal mental model engineers use when reasoning about which layer a problem lives in. The seven layers, bottom-up, are Physical (L1), Data Link (L2), Network (L3), Transport (L4), Session (L5), Presentation (L6), and Application (L7). A useful mnemonic for the exam room is "Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away" — Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application. Each layer communicates logically with its peer on the remote host through a Protocol Data Unit (PDU): L1 carries bits, L2 frames, L3 packets, L4 segments (or datagrams for UDP), and L5–L7 carry simply "data." This PDU naming matters because it tells you, instantly, whether an engineer is talking about a flaky cable (bits), a MAC misconfiguration (frames), a routing black hole (packets), or a TCP socket leak (segments).

Why does the OSI model matter in real systems? Because every debugging conversation in a production outage eventually decomposes into layers. When a Kubernetes pod cannot reach a database, the answer lives somewhere across L1–L7, and the model gives you a vocabulary to bisect the search space: is DNS resolving (L7)? Is the TCP three-way handshake completing (L4)? Is the IP route present (L3)? Is the ARP table populated (L2)? Without this vocabulary, debugging degrades into "is it the network or the app?" — a question that is almost always wrong because the real fault sits at a specific layer. The model also clarifies which tool to reach for: `ping` tests L3, `traceroute` tests L3 hops, `tcpdump` captures L2–L4 frames, `curl` exercises L7, and `nslookup`/`dig` test L7 DNS. Choosing the right tool shortens mean-time-to-resolution (MTTR) dramatically.

Real-world mapping: Kubernetes networking is best understood as an OSI sandwich. A Kubernetes **Service** with `type: ClusterIP` operates at L4 — it is a stable virtual IP backed by `kube-proxy` iptables/IPVS rules that load-balance TCP/UDP connections across pods. A Kubernetes **Ingress** operates at L7 — it terminates HTTP(S) and routes by hostname or URL path, typically implemented by NGINX, Envoy, or HAProxy. The Container Network Interface (CNI) plugin (Calico, Cilium, Flannel) operates at L2/L3 — it assigns each pod an IP and programs the data plane so that packets from one pod reach another, often using VXLAN (L2-over-UDP) or BGP (L3). AWS VPC maps similarly: subnets are L2 broadcast domains emulated by AWS's hypervisor, Route Tables are L3, Security Groups are stateful L4 firewalls, and an Application Load Balancer is L7. Knowing this mapping lets you read a cluster manifest and predict which layer a failure will surface in.

The trade-off: the OSI model is descriptive, not prescriptive, and the boundaries leak badly in practice. TLS is officially L6 (Presentation) but is almost always implemented in the application (L7) and negotiated over a TCP socket (L4). NAT is a classic L3 function but mutates L4 port numbers. Modern load balancers like Envoy or AWS ALB operate at L7 but also do L4 connection pooling. Engineers who insist on placing every technology in exactly one layer will argue for hours; the practical move is to use OSI as a starting vocabulary and accept that real systems blur the lines. Another pitfall is forgetting that lower layers fail silently and kill upper layers: a duplicated L2 MAC address will manifest as intermittent L7 HTTP timeouts, and an MTU mismatch (L2) will cause L4 TCP connections to stall on large packets but succeed on small ones — a notoriously hard class of bug to diagnose without the layered mental model.

OSI connects to nearly every other system design concept: it underlies TCP/IP (Topic 2), HTTP (Topic 3), HTTPS (Topic 4), DNS, load balancing (Phase 5), and the message-queue transports in Phase 7. When you reason about latency budgets, the layered overhead (TCP headers, TLS records, HTTP framing) is the floor of what is physically achievable. When you design for availability (Phase 1, Topic 4), redundant paths at L2/L3 (bonded NICs, BGP multi-path) are the substrate that upper-layer failover depends on. The model is foundational — get it wrong, and every later concept becomes harder to reason about.

### Mermaid Diagram ```mermaid flowchart TD A["L7 Application
HTTP, DNS, gRPC, SSH"] B["L6 Presentation
TLS, JSON, Protobuf, JPEG"] C["L5 Session
Sockets, RPC sessions, NetBIOS"] D["L4 Transport
TCP, UDP, QUIC"] E["L3 Network
IP, ICMP, OSPF, BGP"] F["L2 Data Link
Ethernet, ARP, MAC, VLAN"] G["L1 Physical
Twisted pair, fiber, Wi-Fi radios"] A --> B B --> C C --> D D --> E E --> F F --> G H["PDU: Data"] -.-> A I["PDU: Segments"] -.-> D J["PDU: Packets"] -.-> E K["PDU: Frames"] -.-> F L["PDU: Bits"] -.-> G ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` +------------------------------------------+ | L7 Application | HTTP, gRPC, DNS | PDU: Data +------------------------------------------+ | L6 Presentation | TLS, JSON, Protobuf | PDU: Data +------------------------------------------+ | L5 Session | Sockets, RPC sessions | PDU: Data +------------------------------------------+ | L4 Transport | TCP, UDP, QUIC | PDU: Segment +------------------------------------------+ | L3 Network | IP, ICMP, BGP, OSPF | PDU: Packet +------------------------------------------+ | L2 Data Link | Ethernet, ARP, VLAN | PDU: Frame +------------------------------------------+ | L1 Physical | Copper, fiber, radio | PDU: Bit +------------------------------------------+ Sender: L7 --> L6 --> L5 --> L4 --> L3 --> L2 --> L1 (encapsulate) Receiver: L1 --> L2 --> L3 --> L4 --> L5 --> L6 --> L7 (decapsulate) Kubernetes mapping: +-------+-------------------+--------------------------------+ | Layer | K8s concept | Implementation | +-------+-------------------+--------------------------------+ | L7 | Ingress | NGINX / Envoy / Contour | | L4 | Service (ClusterIP| kube-proxy iptables/IPVS | | L3 | Pod networking | CNI: Calico BGP / Cilium eBPF | | L2 | Pod-to-pod L2 | VXLAN / Geneve overlay | +-------+-------------------+--------------------------------+ ``` ### Walkthrough 1. The sending application at L7 hands data down; each layer adds its own header (encapsulation). L4 adds a TCP header (port, seq), L3 adds an IP header (src/dst IP), L2 adds an Ethernet header (MAC, ethertype), L1 converts to bits on the wire. 2. The receiver reverses the process: L1 reads bits, L2 strips the frame and verifies the FCS, L3 routes the packet, L4 reassembles the segment and delivers it to the right socket, and L7 sees the original payload. 3. Each layer speaks only to its peer: the TCP stack on host A logically talks to the TCP stack on host B, oblivious to which routers forwarded the IP packets in between.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
"""
OSI Layer Packet Dissector (mock).

Pretends to parse a byte buffer that came off the wire and prints which OSI
layer each protocol header belongs to. This is NOT a real dissector (no actual
byte parsing of TCP/IP/Ethernet), it is a teaching mock that demonstrates the
layer-to-protocol mapping and the PDU name changes as data moves up the stack.
"""

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import List

@dataclass
class Layer:
    number: int
    name: str
    pdu: str
    protocols: List[str] = field(default_factory=list)

OSI_LAYERS = [
    Layer(7, "Application",  "Data",     ["HTTP", "DNS", "gRPC", "SSH", "MQTT"]),
    Layer(6, "Presentation", "Data",     ["TLS 1.3", "JSON", "Protobuf", "JPEG"]),
    Layer(5, "Session",      "Data",     ["Sockets", "RPC", "NetBIOS"]),
    Layer(4, "Transport",    "Segment",  ["TCP", "UDP", "QUIC", "SCTP"]),
    Layer(3, "Network",      "Packet",   ["IPv4", "IPv6", "ICMP", "OSPF", "BGP"]),
    Layer(2, "Data Link",    "Frame",    ["Ethernet", "ARP", "VLAN", "Wi-Fi"]),
    Layer(1, "Physical",     "Bit",      ["Twisted pair", "Fiber", "Radio"]),
]

def dissect(observed_protocols: List[str]) -> None:
    """Given a list of protocols seen in a capture, classify each into its OSI layer."""
    print(f"{'Proto':<12}{'Layer':<22}{'PDU':<10}")
    print("-" * 44)
    seen_layers = set()
    for proto in observed_protocols:
        matched = None
        for layer in OSI_LAYERS:
            if proto in layer.protocols:
                matched = layer
                break
        if matched is None:
            print(f"{proto:<12}{'(unknown)':<22}{'?':<10}")
            continue
        seen_layers.add(matched.number)
        print(f"{proto:<12}L{matched.number} {matched.name:<19}{matched.pdu:<10}")

    # Diagnose the highest layer reached by this conversation.
    # In our numbering, higher layer number == closer to the user (L7 = top).
    if seen_layers:
        top = max(seen_layers)
        top_layer = next(l for l in OSI_LAYERS if l.number == top)
        print(f"\nHighest layer reached: L{top} ({top_layer.name})")
        print("Implies an end-to-end application session was established.")

def k8s_layer_map() -> None:
    """Show how Kubernetes concepts map onto OSI layers."""
    print("\nKubernetes -> OSI mapping")
    print("-" * 60)
    k8s = [
        ("Ingress (HTTP routing)",       7, "NGINX/Envoy/Contour"),
        ("Service: ClusterIP/NodePort",  4, "kube-proxy iptables/IPVS"),
        ("Pod IP routing",                3, "Calico BGP / Cilium eBPF"),
        ("Pod-to-pod overlay",            2, "VXLAN / Geneve tunnel"),
        ("Node NIC",                      1, "ENI on AWS / virtio on KVM"),
    ]
    for concept, layer, impl in k8s:
        print(f"L{layer} | {concept:<32} | {impl}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Example: a typical HTTPS request observed on the wire
    capture = ["Ethernet", "ARP", "IPv4", "TCP", "TLS 1.3", "HTTP", "DNS"]
    print("=== Packet dissector (observed protocols) ===")
    dissect(capture)

    print()
    k8s_layer_map()
```

quiz.question: What are the seven OSI layers and what PDU does each one use?
options: At L2, the unit on the wire is a frame — Ethernet header plus payload plus FCS, addressed by MAC.
Encapsulation means each layer wraps the upper-layer PDU with its own header (and sometimes trailer) before handing it down.
L3 (Network) is responsible for end-to-end delivery across multiple hops using logical IP addresses and routing protocols like OSPF and BGP.
Bottom-up they are Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, and Application — memorized as "Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away." The PDU names change only for…
quiz.explanation: Bottom-up they are Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, and Application — memorized as "Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away." The PDU names change only for the bottom four layers: L1 carries bits, L2 frames, L3 packets, and L4 segments (or datagrams for UDP).

quiz.question: What is the difference between a frame, a packet, and a segment?
options: L3 (Network) is responsible for end-to-end delivery across multiple hops using logical IP addresses and routing protocols like OSPF and BGP.
Encapsulation means each layer wraps the upper-layer PDU with its own header (and sometimes trailer) before handing it down.
Bottom-up they are Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, and Application — memorized as "Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away." The PDU names change only for…
At L2, the unit on the wire is a frame — Ethernet header plus payload plus FCS, addressed by MAC.
quiz.explanation: They are the same chunk of data described at three different layers. At L2, the unit on the wire is a frame — Ethernet header plus payload plus FCS, addressed by MAC. When the L3 header is examined, the same bytes are called a packet, addressed by IP.

quiz.question: Which OSI layer does TLS belong to, and why is the answer controversial?
options: This is a classic L4-vs-L7 termination trade-off.
Connection reset" is an L4 TCP RST — the peer (or a middlebox) actively tore down the connection.
DNS resolving means L7 DNS over UDP/TCP succeeded, so L3 (routing) and L4 (transport) work for DNS at least.
Officially, TLS lives at L6 (Presentation) because it encrypts, decrypts, and formats data on behalf of the application — exactly the textbook role of the Presentation…
quiz.explanation: Officially, TLS lives at L6 (Presentation) because it encrypts, decrypts, and formats data on behalf of the application — exactly the textbook role of the Presentation layer. In practice, TLS is almost always implemented inside the application itself (L7) and runs over a TCP socket (L4), with no separate Presentation component.

quiz.question: Why does the OSI model use encapsulation, and what does it buy us?
options: Because OSI is the better pedagogical model.
At L2, the unit on the wire is a frame — Ethernet header plus payload plus FCS, addressed by MAC.
Officially, TLS lives at L6 (Presentation) because it encrypts, decrypts, and formats data on behalf of the application — exactly the textbook role of the Presentation…
Encapsulation means each layer wraps the upper-layer PDU with its own header (and sometimes trailer) before handing it down.
quiz.explanation: Encapsulation means each layer wraps the upper-layer PDU with its own header (and sometimes trailer) before handing it down. The benefit is strict separation of concerns: TCP doesn't care whether it's running over IPv4 or IPv6; IP doesn't care whether its payload is TCP or UDP; Ethernet doesn't care whether it's carrying IP or ARP.

quiz.question: How does the OSI model differ from the TCP/IP model in layer count?
options: Start at L3 because VPC Peering is fundamentally an L3 construct — it adds routes between two VPCs without L2 connectivity.
Connection reset" is an L4 TCP RST — the peer (or a middlebox) actively tore down the connection.
ping succeeding proves L3 (ICMP) works, so the IP route is present and both nodes are reachable at the network layer.
OSI has seven layers; TCP/IP collapses them into four. The TCP/IP Application layer absorbs OSI's Application, Presentation, and Session (L7+L6+L5).
quiz.explanation: OSI has seven layers; TCP/IP collapses them into four. The TCP/IP Application layer absorbs OSI's Application, Presentation, and Session (L7+L6+L5). The TCP/IP Transport layer maps directly to OSI L4.
